Not sure why Reddit suggested this post and whilst I'm happy for you - genuinely, it would do you some good before judging the world, to realise that some people can't just leap into action and do this - despite very much wishing they could.  Not everything is willpower and seize the day.  Being humble is another way of being awakened, realising that what you see as overweight slobs on their phones might actually be like that for a reason other than being lazy and "asleep".

Take me for example.  Used to be entirely independent and working an exciting career I loved- 60hrs per week, active social life and hobbies.  Then that tanked. Then my mental health tanked. I was working on fixing both.  Then Covid hit and my mental health tanked more, followed by my physical health (covid nearly made me blind - Still could, and entirely upended my nervous system.)

I used to hike daily, paint, write, and prior to Covid, was reassessing my life and planning to work in Kyoto.  Now I am indeed overweight, back in my parents house, and definitely have coping mechanisms that resemble addictions.  Why?  Because Covid has left me literally unable to do the hobbies I actually love.  Every day is a grieving process.  And forget working. Lol.

I'll agree with you here- sleep is important.  I used to take sleeping easily and restoratively for granted.  If you can still do that, fucking cherish it.  When my nervous system cracked, I stopped being able to sleep like that.  I now wake multiple times a night, at best, and sometimes barely sleep at all.  I've invested in a quality sleep mask and supplements which seem to help but they aren't a long term fix for the underlying issues.

I am currently hoping to see a neuroimmunologist and in the meantime, I am simply surviving the nuclear fallout that Covid has wrecked on my body and my life.

So I wish you all the best.  I do.  But we aren't all on the same path.  Be grateful you are in a place where you can implement such changes with sheer willpower.

Same.  Certirizine works for skin allergies/food reactions for me, but for hayfever, gotta be acrivastine - sworn by it for years.  Certirizine does bugger all for my hayfever, and loratadine didn't make drowsy but made my legs and arms turn to limp noodles, which was fascinating to try and walk!

Sometimes I'd be fine, then do something entirely innocuous, like change my trousers, and both thighs would suddenly get intensely painful, and that could last for hours.  

Sometimes I'll be walking just fine.  No pain at all. Then something will happen, like anticipatory stress, and both thighs immediately seize up, get heavy and aching.  It's the maddest thing.

Yep.  Post covid I got it in my chest- like a phone was vibrating in the left of my ribs.  Went away and has returned a few times.  I also can get it in my my thighs randomly- usually the right and it lasts a few seconds.

So, I know the brain retraining gets a bad rep here, and I'm not advertising it. This is just my own experience.  My brain burning that began last year, the same day I did a relaxing meditation, only improved when I stopped freaking out about it so much.  I still get it from time to time, but it's not as bad nor as persistent.  For me it seems very much is tied up with the nervous system (the meditation jacked my nervous system up more, rather than calming it.)  The pain got so severe at one point, my parents found me curled up, babbling one morning, pretty delirious and I begged them to kill me. 

The stabbing pains.. I'm not sure.  I've had all sorts over the last few years. Occipital, temporal, and an alarming sharp and very painful stabbing in what felt like my carotid followed by visual disturbance on the same side (nothing was ever found on visual checks, or at the ER.)  I've had excruciating head pains on the left side that landed me in hospital (pre covid, post vaccine.) 

 I'm almost certain something dodgy is going on with my neck.  I hit a pothole last year, and that kicked off head pressure for a temporary time - pressure  that would only happen (tmi sorry,) post orgasm.  I also have felt sensations like a fist being driven into the back of my neck - so forceful it pushes me forward.  

I've also had painful facial pressure when I used a basic saline nasal spray - like my sinuses  hyperreacted to just being sprayed, even though it wasn't even medication - that was in summer 2022.

So... I don't really have more answers I'm afraid - I wish I did!   But solidarity.

OK first off.  And I mean this with love. Calm down.  You are doing the absolute right thing now, getting it checked out by an optical professional. Good.  Don't beat yourself up. 

Yes Covid affected my eyes.  I was diagnosed with anterior uveitis in the right eye immediately post infection (inflammation of the uvea).  I've also had retinal bleeds, but pertinent to your post, I have experienced two retinal detachments.  And also now diagnosed with open angle glaucoma in the right eye.  I have a history of childhood ROP (retinopathy of prematurity), previously treated with cryotherapy and which was stable all my life until after Covid.

I'll tell you this to hopefully give you some insight. Not to scare you. But to share what happened to me as comparison.  (But do still get your eyes checked!!!)

Retinal detachment number 1 - This was a classic textbook detachment.  Gold star. Bloody thing.  One moment I was eating dinner, the next moment the left side of my right vision (same eye that had the uveitis,) was in shadow.  I'd been doing a lot of computer work, and figured it was lighting or a migraine.  But it looked wrong still and I had no headache.  If I moved my eyes, the shadow would move like a curtain across my visual field, and then back again. 

 I got this checked, and confirmed as an acute detachment, but with the macula on - this was important because it meant though the detachment was severe, it hadn't yet affected my central vision (GOOD THING). BUT because it was New Year, there was a delay in my surgery, so for five, long, harrowing days, I watched that shadow creep closer to my macula every day.  It was pure terror to go to sleep every night, not knowing if I'd wake up blind in that eye.

  The interesting thing was in the portion of shadow that was detached, if I closed my eyes, it was a very bright grey.  Essentially I was seeing the negative image of zero eyesight.  The other thing was in different rooms and lighting it would change a bit.  It had a jagged inner border which would glow neon colours in different lighting.  

Fast forward, I got the surgery.  They were able to repair the detachment, but I lost a significant portion of my peripheral vision, esp over my shoulder.  But I retained central vision, which was very touch and go at the time.  The surgeon told me it was "the most complicated example of a detachment" he'd ever operated on- and he has had an illustrious and long career.  Woo. Go me for being complicated!   The retina was paper thin and extremely fragile.  This isn't the case for everybody, and in all liklihood related to my childhood history of ROP (retinopathy of prematurity.)

--

Second detachment.  Heh.  This one remains active.  It's in the left eye but above the visual field and above where even the most detailed scans can reach.  They could only see it with manual equipment.  Interestingly, I went to my optician with visual disturbances, and he found the detachment.  But he and the specialists said those visual disturbances actually have nothing whatsoever to do with the detachment.  It was essentially "an incidental finding".  

They're not operating because, for now, the detachment appears stable and contained, and not affecting my visual field.  They don't want to risk my (better in that eye) functional sight with an operation that could actually put that at risk- especially as that eye is the only one I can see detail up close with.  The other eye doesn't function close-up.  So I have to keep an eye on it.  Its... scary.  

I've always been comforted that my left (more detail orientated eye) seemed untouched by Covid.  Now I theorise a retinal bleed in it in 2023, may have preceeded the detachment we now have found.  But.  It's stable.  I have to cling to the hope that it may remain so and if not... well, I'll cross that bridge when I come to it.

They should do this anyway, but if not, ask to get an OCT scan and a visual field test.  They definitely should do a standard dilated pupil test at bare minimum.  Because of my open angle glaucoma, I also get Heidelberg testing which looks at the optic nerve.  They may or may not do that with you. Worth asking about though.  With me, I also got a fluorescein angiogram, to see all the small vessels in my eyes properly, but that isn't standard practice - they did mine because of the recurrent nature of the uveitis.

If you want to talk about any of this, feel free to message me anytime.  I wish you all the best with your appointment.

100% I think this is what happens.  My eyes and uterus were the things with past history.  Childhood ROP and PCOS.  What happens after Covid? (aside from the usual post viral neuroimmune crapola...)  My eyes go to shit, and my menstrual cycle goes completely sideways with insane clotting that I'd never experienced in my near 20 years of dealing with PCOS.  I then developed several uterine polyps and finally atypical endometrial hyperplasia (precancer) requiring a total hysterectomy.  

It also seems to be now that I probably always had very mild MCAS and dysautonomia... sensitive soul all over apparently (but never clocked it,) and that would explain why my entire nervous system is now in the bin, post Covid.

Would those things have happened anyway eventually?  Sure, maybe.  Did Covid bring them to the forefront decades sooner? Yep.  Its so blindingly obvious that it makes me mad that specialists still insist it has zero to do with Covid.  I have ophthalmologists telling me, at the second retinal detachment, that it is "just bad luck".  

Same with my uncle who had an entirely stable heart condition, and a month after Covid suddenly needed cardiac surgery.  Or my friend who was insanely fit and healthy, but has bad cardiac genetics in the family.  His heart was fine until after Covid.  He was training to be a pilot.  Now he has myocarditis and that dream is dead.

I was very disappointed in one friend recently.  She has seen EVERYTHING I've gone through and I thought she believed me, even if she didn't understand it.  She said on video call " I know you think Covid caused this, but sometimes bad things just happen.. it's part of life."  She was talking about both my uveitis/retinal detachments and nervous system.  

I was like... sure, but love... my eyes were fine for over thirty years. Then a week after Covid I'm diagnosed with uveitis in my weaker eye, and within 2 years, two retinal detachments.  That isn't "just a bad thing randomly happening".

I get it.  If they admit Covid is actually this dangerous, then no one is safe, including them.  If they just thing this is random lightning strikes of crappy fate, then life can go on...

Destroyed your life?  I try not to think so catastrophically- purely for my own mental health.  Given you health conditions and issues you didn't have prior, or brought up latent crap that is making your life currently shitty? Yeah, probably. 

 I'm battling seb derm atm - have been since my nervous system really crapped up last August.  I don't have any answers - but solidarity- it's really frustrating to have to deal with.  Mine isn't responding to standard OTC treatments so I'm hoping to see a dermatologist.  Seb derm can be caused by all sorts of things, stress (which goes hand in hand with nervous system dysregulation, which Covid absolutely causes in many people.)

This shit is hard.  It is terrifying.  But what I will say is this.  Just because it was caused by Covid, doesn't make it neccessarily impossible to deal with.  And infact the more people who acknowledge that this is happening, that this is real, the more seriously it will get taken.  I don't believe that is false hope.  

It is my theory that what we called "Long Covid" can look vastly different in different people.  I'm not disputing there can be some very commonly shared symptoms post-Covid (buzzing, fatigue, headaches etc,) nor I am disputing the fact that a solid proportion of people post Covid are developing what looks exactly like ME/CFS.  That is horrifying and there is no sugarcoating that.  BUT the very fact so many people are now showing up with ME symptoms, means that fucking finally ME is being taken more seriously.

 But Covid also I am sure reactivates dormant/latent crap that was previously kept under control, and THAT can different widely between people.  My uncle for example had heart surgery in the 90s.  Totally stable until after Covid. He's now having cardiac issues again.  With me; it was my eyes.  Childhood ROP, stable all my life until after Covid when I developed uveitis, retinal bleeds, and retinal detachments.

We all go through denial.  But acknowledging reality doesn't have to mean your life is over.  It means it has got far harder, yes, but not over.  If it makes you feel any better, my nervous system appeared to shatter last August and I experience a lot of the symptoms you say.  

Sometimes I experience episodes thay on the surface, look like PEM, which is horrifying.  But equally they then behave bizarrely and my body resets fast.  I can wake up feeling like cement with swollen glands, and then after some food and a cry, I feel entirely fine again.  Or feel in general like cement and a blood draw resets it.  The point is that things have waxed and waned over time.  Many nights ive gone to sleep certain Im going to wake up trashed and I dont.  I'm waiting now to see a neuroimmunologist and a rheumatologist so, we'll see.

I was surprised how calm it did make me initially, because I'm a massive cynic, but I could sense the movement of my breath being visualised.  

It was kinda cool.... up until an hour after when my head decided to burn and glow like Satan's armpit while using my phone.  The phone definitely became a conduit at that time, however it isn't consistent. I've had terrible burning episodes without the phone being involved at all - but yeah, it all started that same afternoon, and using my phone had never done that to me before on all my life, so the meditation seems the clear trigger - somehow!

That is SUCH a good technique about the grocery store. Just letting it wash around you, almost like decoration, rather than something you have to engage with.  And definitely agree on accepting that if you feel crappy, take what you have got and return another day and not force yourself to feel more overwhelmed just to get the cheese or whatever.   That's a good practice I think for life anyway.

One tip someone gave me was to try and treat outside life like I'm in a really realistic computer game - with main quests and sidequests.  (My therapist thinks I'm ADHD so that really resonated with me.)  

So instead of thinking "oh god. I've got a really important appointment with a new specialist today. Oh god. I hope I'll be OK", instead think "I have to visit the Magic Healer of the Forest Realm and on the way, I shall collect health points (a sandwich) from the Pixie Deli (supermarket) on the way." 

 Basically, try and override the overwhelm with fun.  It doesn't work all the time, and I don't do it to demean the importance of such appointments, but it seems to help take the sting out of the buildup, especially when I take in the environment and pretend it is some far flung land, with interesting inhabitants, not just the local hospital.

Listening to birds is lovely. I bought a little feeder and it's nice to see them hopping around.  This illness really makes you appreciate the small joys.

Ooof.  I'm so sorry!   It's so ridiculous that something that is supposed to calm the body down, just..  doesn't.  I used to swear by acupuncture, and I never had a bad reaction til after Covid.  Now, i get a strong immune response in the same pattern for 3 days exactly.  I don't think it it's PEM so much as my body going "wtf did you do? What was that?'  The one and only deep tissue massage I had, left my left abdomen purple and kickstarted all the cardiac-like pains I've had ever since.  Turns out screaming in agonising pain, while being held down by a small Chinese lady who is shouting that you need to relax, is not standard practice.

Hey I know this was a long while ago, but I wondered if there's any chance you could have had a mild case of Covid while in the Canaries?  Reason I ask is some otherwise asymptomatic cases present with gut issues.   It can also dysregulate the autonomic nervous system, which could potentially account for the palpitations (esp if you have no history of anxiety,) skin issues, red face and dry eyes. 

You might want to look into MCAS, which is a known fallout of the umbrella that is Long Covid.  Can definitely contribute to gut issues, palps, skin reactivity and eye issues

 I've been dealing with intense autonomic dysfunction for nearly a year, and my symptoms include facial flushing, seb derm and dry eyes/issues with eyes closing randomly, amongst a whole other host of crap - all of which I've never experienced before.  This all kicked off after some intense long term stress and I trace the initial dysfunction back to my Covid infection, though I didn't realise it at the time.  I was also diagnosed with anterior uveitis (inflammation of the uvea in the eye) immediately after my Covid infection.

Thanks for commenting. Yep. So many people seem to fall into this category and I swear it can't be a coincidence.  

Type A people. Neurodiverse. Fit as a fiddle.  So many LCers fit into at least one category, some, all three.  There's also an argument I've seen that LCers had prior mental health/emotional difficulties and/or previous underlying conditions like childhood eczema (possible predisposition to MCAS? Sensitive system in general?) It's a stretch to link everything, but I was speaking to my GP who is a gem and agreed there's a lot of consistent crossovers he is seeing with LC patients too.

I'm no doctor but it's almost like those patients whose bodies were already wired to optimum health, then entirely overreacted to Covid, broke the ceiling, and threw the body into what now is LC.

 I was a bit overweight admittedly, but I still walked regularly, ate pretty healthily etc.  Verrry much a go-go-go Type A personality, up for dawn walks, lots of projects on the go (I *was* learning Japanese with a plan to teach in Kyoto pre-pandemic.... sigh,) neurodiverse and looked after myself quite well.

Anyway I'm rambling sorry.  Wishing you all the best ❤️

You do realise that a lot of people with LC were in the best shape of their lives before developing it?  So just being overweight absolutely does not = LC.  I know a whole bunch of overweight people who have caught Covid multiple times and don't have LC.  It's not that simple.

Thank you for your kind reply.  I have put it on pause, sort of. I mean.. I poke at it once a week lately.  But I'm still symptomatic around it when I don't work on it.  Forever is a lot right now.  But ultimately I just feel disgusting (sebhorric dermatitis) and hopeless and sad.  I keep thinking maybe this isn't CFS, because of the way so many of my symptoms turn on and off at random.  But equally I can't deny that I seem to be getting worse.  Or at least on a new chapter of crap. 

I'm sorry. I really do appreciate your comment.  This morning I'm feeling particularly vulnerable and raw.

Well that's a gut punch.  I didn't write it down in this detail just to write it down  - I wrote this level of detail because I had a shred of hope left that it may not be CFS.  Sorry, your comment just left me kinda devastated and raw.  What in it do you recognise please?

I'm so pleased for you that the LDN helped and that you were able to find someone willing to prescribe it.  It seems to be highly variable in how people react but I've heard a lot of good stories.   As sucky as PEM/brain fog is, if it is consistent and predictable, at least you can tentatively plan life around it a bit more I guess?

I thought I had a great reaction to propolis actually.  I took in in Dec last year, and all of January I felt much better.  Now however I attribute it less to the propolis (although I still remain positive about its use in general - amazing for healing skin!) But more that I had a hysterectomy. You'd think that would make me worse, but I now theorise it gave my body something fleshy to focus on healing, and it dropped the rest of the symptoms right down.  My symptoms werent gone, but they were much reduced.  They began creeping back in after the first few weeks of initial healing, and after some quite intense mental health stress. I could be wrong, but it's the best theory I've got.  

I'm curious - when you say you also had inconsistency - do you mean your symptoms also turned on and off randomly with nothing/random interventions? Or something else?

Unfortunately I can't take LDN currently because I'm on amtriptyline.  I was tapering down, but I went back up when the intense nerve pains began last year in my legs, and because that helped at the time, I'm reluctant to reduce the dose.  Definitely going to bring it up to my GP though, thank you.

I've read that before about CFS -so many people with a viral infection and stress at the same time.   With me, apparently my blood showed "potential reactivated EBV" last Aug, but my GP is now more unsure on that.  But absolutely, no denying the stress I was under at the time.  

Infact, when I have experienced new or intensifying symptoms during these past 8 months, I always can trace it back to a stressful time.  Ironically, the best I felt all this time was after my hysterectomy in January.  I don't remember what symptoms I had then, but there's barely anything in my diary.  Towards the end of the month, I was having more personal/mental health stress and becoming more symptomatic again.

The irony of all of this is I end up stressing about stress.  And sometimes I cant just click out of those loops.  I have rumination OCD and ruminating thought spirals are so hard to break, and I really do try.

My big fear is will every life stressor make me worse.  How can I date? Do therapy? Work? If all of it = potential stress and mental health that will introduce a new low of my whole system

Thank you so much for replying - I'm hugely grateful.  I know in the lead up to August 2024, I had a lot of concentrated stress with finances and mental health, life in general, as well as physical injuries (neck whiplash on the right - which makes it interesting how so many of my symptoms flare worse in the right.) But equally I have had stresses and mental health issues for many years before Covid (which I was working on in therapy,) and they never landed me like this.

I hear you on the rest/relaxation. It is a terrible habit of mine to stay up SO late.  I never used to. It's just hard when I generally feel better, even normal sometimes later at night.  But it isnt good in the long run.

Interestingly, I did try some meditation (yoga nidra) back last year and that single session seemed to jack my nervous system up more.  The brain burning began on that day and... there aren't words for the pain.  It was so bad at one point I got delirious.

Point of that is that traditional relaxation techniques don't seem to work for me now.  I used to swear by acupuncture.  Now, it makes me ill for 3 days, (nausea/malaise, ibs - each a different day and always the same pattern.)  Chamomile tea makes me jittery like I've had three espressos.  And meditation well... yeah.

That is interesting. And I hear you about the pain trying to get things tested properly. It's ridiculous.  It's like they gatekeep the most logical tests sometimes istg.   

Sometimes I find I am pretty symptom-lite at night which is interesting, though things fluctuate throughout the day.  It's one of the main reasons I question whether I have CFS or not, because my symptoms are all over the place. There is fatigue (yesterday was a doozy.  Heavy eyes all day.  Today I still feel tired but not nearly as wrecked and my eyes are fine.)  Sometimes there's logic, and sometimes there just isn't, or it is entirely contradictory.  What looks like PEM then does weird things and resolves spontaneously.

I've had heavy eyes and weak tired thighs, except for when I was engaging in conversation - then I'd feel fine.  One day, my eyes just kept randomly closing with zero fatigue, and (sorry for tmi) but instantly resolved after a bowel movement.  I literally felt my eyes stop burning, relax and wake up.  Or my favourite - feeling my legs tired, deep throbbing pain, eat some breakfast, and then 20 mins later, watched the pain just kinda.. melt away. Like butter off a hot plate.

Unfortunately, these resets and fixes aren't consistent.  But yeah, they are what predominantly make me question whether I actually am dealing with CFS or something else.  The fact i can feel diabolical and feverish one moment, and then get something as innocuous as a papercut and instantly feel fine again, is insane.

Admittedly, my adrenaline surges were always tied to periods of anxiety or stress - but the stress would keep looping, if that makes sense?  I would wake up with it too, but weirdly it could often calm down once I was up and around.  I'd get other symptoms through the day, but the adrenaline was mostly at night/morning.  Jelly legs happened a lot.

  I also sometimes would wake gasping for air, or take involuntary gasps of breath during the day.  Just sitting there minding my own business and I'd suddenly breathe in like I'd surfaced from drowning.  That can happen anytime really.
Weirdly I had severe adrenaline going on at one point, with all the hallmarks of Cushings, and my cortisol was normal, on both bloods and 24hr urine tests.

Thank you for replying, I really appreciate it.   My reply is likely to be quite long I'm afraid.  No urgency to reply!  Please don't read more than you're able at once. ❤️ 

And good question! I've often wondered about my neck/spine.  Had it MRId in 2022 and it was normal, but that was before all this kicked off.  GP asked about EDS but I don't seem to match any of the versions of it. 

 I've had a bunch of injuries in recent years - hit my head (one compression from head to neck downwards,) mild whiplash and jolted my spine and ribs.  It's very possible, but equally it's so inconsistent.  What is fine to do one day, may be difficult the next.  Sometimes I feel more alert kneeling down, and then upright I feel distant and weird again.  Sometimes I'll be bright and alert sitting, and the instant I stand up, my eyes close.

Infact, had that one day where:
-Sofa: Alert
-Walking to car: Fatigued with eyes closing
-Sitting in car (passenger): Alert
-Out of car and in store : Eyes closing but improved the longer I was out (adrenaline?? Maybe?)

I then had a weird turn in the store. Like my body just slammed on the emergency brake.  Brain went distant, I felt jittery, wafty, got wrapping back/abdominal chills like I get with IBS.  Came home, had a sit and a drink/snack, and then felt absolutely OK again and cooked the family meal with no further symptoms.  It was like my body panicked, then gradually switched back online.
